prompt: Who decides which files an editor assistant's model sees?
hint: Lesson 1 said the model sees only the request.

choices.text: The model, which reads the repository it needs
choices.why: The model reads nothing by itself; it gets a request.

choices.text: The provider, from a copy of your repository it keeps
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson keeps a copy of the project.

choices.text: The editor tool, when it builds each request
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nobody; every file in the project goes into every request
choices.why: A budget of 3,000 tokens would not hold that.

prompt: Sending the code before the cursor and the code after it, so the model fills the gap between them, is called fill-in-the-___.
hint: Three words, the last one missing.

prompt: How many tokens of context did the first `assist complete` send?
hint: The first line it printed.

prompt: A completion keeps calling `apply_discount()`, which does not exist; the project's function is `apply_coupon()` in `shop/coupons.py`. What does the section suggest checking first?
hint: What did the model have in front of it?

choices.text: Whether `shop/coupons.py` was in the context at all, as a tab or a named file
choices.why: Right. Opening it in a tab is the first fix to try.

choices.text: Whether the model's training cutoff is before the function was written
choices.why: The function is in your project, not in the training data either way.

choices.text: Whether the temperature is too high for code
choices.why: Inventing a plausible name is a missing-context problem first.

choices.text: Whether the budget is set to more than 3,000 tokens
choices.why: A bigger budget helps only if the file was being dropped, which is what the first check finds out.

prompt: `.env` is listed in `.gitignore`. What does that do about an assistant reading it?

choices.text: It stops every assistant from reading it
choices.why: git's list is git's; the editor opens any file.

choices.text: It encrypts the file on disk
choices.why: `.gitignore` changes nothing about the file itself.

choices.text: It makes the provider discard the file after use
choices.why: The provider never sees your `.gitignore`.

choices.text: Nothing: it only keeps the file out of commits
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Why did `PAYMENTS_KEY = "pk_lab_…"` get past `assist`'s secret check while `.env` did not?
hint: What does the check look at?

choices.text: Python files are never checked
choices.why: `settings.py` was checked; it passed.

choices.text: Its name was not on the pattern's list
choices.why: Right. The check matches names like token or api_key; a pattern sees a shape, not a fact.

choices.text: The value was too short to be a secret
choices.why: It is sixteen characters after the prefix, over the eight the pattern asks for.

choices.text: labllm removed the key before logging it
choices.why: The key is in the log: `grep -c` found it once.

prompt: A real key was sent to a model provider by mistake. What does the section say to do?
hint: Can a request be called back?

choices.text: Ask the provider to delete the request from its logs
choices.why: There is no way to call a request back, and nothing to verify.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the key was in a test file
choices.why: A key is a key wherever it was typed.

choices.text: Revoke it and issue a new one straight away
choices.why: Right. Treat the old one as public.

choices.text: Add the file to `.gitignore`
choices.why: That keeps it out of commits and does nothing about what was sent.

prompt: Which of these does the section count as protection against sending a secret? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four rules close the section.

choices.text: Keeping secrets out of files the editor opens
choices.why: Yes, and it is the one that does most.

choices.text: A committed exclusion list naming where secrets live
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A longer secret, so the pattern check catches it
choices.why: Length was never the hole; the name was.

choices.text: Rotating a secret that did leave
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Why did ana write the tests for `remove()` from its docstring and not from the suggested code?
hint: What would a test written from the code check?

choices.text: Because the suggested code had no comments to read
choices.why: Comments are not the issue.

choices.text: A test read off the code checks nothing new
choices.why: Right: it only checks that the code does what it does.

choices.text: Because pytest cannot import code written by an assistant
choices.why: pytest imports any code.

choices.text: To save tokens on the next request
choices.why: The tests were not sent to the model.

prompt: How many of the four tests in `tests/test_remove.py` failed against the suggestion?
hint: The last line of the run.

prompt: What does the section call the usual shape of a wrong suggestion?
hint: Two tests passed and two failed.

choices.text: Wrong from the first line, which makes it easy to spot
choices.why: The first lines were right here.

choices.text: Badly formatted, so review catches it
choices.why: It was formatted perfectly.

choices.text: Calling functions that do not exist
choices.why: That is a different failure, from lesson 1.

choices.text: Right in the middle, wrong at the edges
choices.why: Right: the edges the docstring named.

prompt: Put ana's way of accepting `remove()` in order.
hint: The intent comes first.
items: Write the signature and the docstring
Fix what fails, and run everything
trap: Writing the tests after reading the suggestion is the usual slip: they end up checking it rather than the docstring.

prompt: How many tokens did `AGENTS.md` add to every completion request?
hint: Its line in the breakdown.

prompt: `AGENTS.md` says money is integer cents. What makes sure the code actually keeps to that?
hint: A request, or a check?

choices.text: The tests, and CI running them
choices.why: Right. The file improves the odds; a check enforces.

choices.text: The instruction file, since the model must obey it
choices.why: It is part of the prompt, which the model continues from, not a rule it is bound by.

choices.text: The model's training on good Python
choices.why: Training knows nothing about this project's rule.

choices.text: Repeating the rule in capitals in the file
choices.why: Emphasis may help the odds; it still enforces nothing.

prompt: Match each line to whether the section would put it in the instruction file.
hint: Four kinds of content are discussed.

pairs.left: Never edit a test to make it pass

right_distractors: Yes: a style rule any developer follows anyway

prompt: After `git apply refactor.diff`, all eight tests passed. Why was that not enough?
hint: What did the eight tests have in common?

choices.text: pytest was run before the patch was applied
choices.why: It ran after; the command is `git apply … && python -m pytest`.

choices.text: A refactoring always needs a hundred tests
choices.why: There is no such number.

choices.text: None covered a coupon near the threshold
choices.why: Right, so none of them saw the change.

choices.text: The diff was applied to the wrong file
choices.why: It changed `shop/cart.py`, as intended.

prompt: A cart of 21,000 cents with the WELCOME10 coupon: what should `total()` return, in cents, under the shop's rule that the threshold is checked after the discount?
hint: Discount, then is 18,900 under 20,000?

prompt: What does the section say to do before asking for a refactoring of code with thin tests?
hint: Pin, then…

choices.text: Ask the assistant to also write tests from the new code
choices.why: Tests read off the new code pin the new behaviour, mistakes included.

choices.text: Write tests that pin the current behaviour, on the old code
choices.why: Right, and commit them first.

choices.text: Raise the context budget so the model sees more
choices.why: More context does not check anything.

choices.text: Refactor in one large commit so it can be reverted at once
choices.why: Keep the refactoring and any behaviour change apart instead.

prompt: What exactly changed in `shipping()` in the assistant's diff?
hint: Compare the two `if` lines.

choices.text: The threshold went from 200.00 to 189.00
choices.why: `FREE_SHIPPING_FROM` did not change.

choices.text: The shipping price went up from 15.00
choices.why: `SHIPPING` did not change.

choices.text: The discount is no longer applied to the total
choices.why: `total()` still subtracts it.

choices.text: The threshold now ignores the discount and looks at the raw subtotal
choices.why: Right: it is compared with the subtotal before the discount.

prompt: The doctest expected `'-0.05'` for `format_price(-5)` and got `___`.
hint: Copy it from the failure, quotes included.

prompt: Why does `format_price(-5)` return `'-1.95'`?

choices.text: `//` rounds down, towards minus infinity
choices.why: Right: the units are -1 and the remainder 95.

choices.text: The docstring changed the function's behaviour
choices.why: A docstring is text; it changed nothing.

choices.text: Negative numbers are converted to floats first
choices.why: Nothing here touches a float.

choices.text: `parse_price` was called by mistake
choices.why: Only `format_price` ran.

prompt: In the doctest failure, which was wrong: the example or the code?
hint: What should a price of minus five cents read as?

choices.text: The example, since the code has run in production without complaints
choices.why: Nobody had ever asked it about a negative amount.

choices.text: Both; neither says what negative prices mean
choices.why: The example states a clear intent, and it is the sensible one.

choices.text: The code: the example states what the function is for, and the code disagrees with it
choices.why: Right. The doctest found a real bug.

choices.text: Neither; doctests are unreliable with negative numbers
choices.why: The doctest compared two strings exactly, as it always does.

prompt: Which parts of a generated docstring does the section say to check against the code? Choose all that apply.
hint: Claims a fluent writer fills in by plausibility.

choices.text: The grammar of its first sentence
choices.why: Grammar is not a claim about the code.

choices.text: The exceptions it says the function raises
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The units of the arguments
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Every example, by running it
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Match each mode to what you review in it.
hint: From a line to a pull request.

pairs.right: A line or a block, as it appears
A reply or a diff, before applying it
The whole change, like a pull request

right_distractors: Nothing; it is checked by the provider

prompt: An agent in a project you have never worked on asks to run commands. Which permission setting does the section recommend to start with?
hint: Slow is safe here.

choices.text: Allow any command, so it can finish without interruptions
choices.why: That lets text the agent read decide what runs on your machine.

choices.text: Approve each edit and each command it wants to run
choices.why: Right, and loosen it on purpose later.

choices.text: Allow commands but forbid file edits
choices.why: Commands can edit files too.

choices.text: Forbid everything and paste its plan into a terminal by hand
choices.why: That is chat with extra steps, and loses the agent's point.

prompt: Why does the section single out security-sensitive code?
hint: Think of the generated `verify_signature`.

choices.text: Assistants refuse to write it
choices.why: They write it readily.

choices.text: It is always longer than other code
choices.why: Length is not the point.

choices.text: Its mistakes pass the obvious tests
choices.why: Right: tests of valid input pass, and the mistake is exploited later.

choices.text: Providers charge more for it
choices.why: Prices are per token, whatever the code is about.

prompt: What does the section suggest using an assistant for while you are learning a language?
hint: Explain, not replace.

choices.text: Completing every exercise, to move faster
choices.why: That teaches you to accept completions.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: It suggests one use.

choices.text: Writing the tests, so you can write the code
choices.why: The section does not say that.

choices.text: Explaining an error, rather than making it go away
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A teammate accepted a forty-line agent change to the checkout, the tests passed, and a week later a customer was charged shipping twice. Which habit from this lesson would most likely have caught it?
hint: What did the passing tests have in common with lesson 3 section 06?

choices.text: Tests pinning the old behaviour first
choices.why: Right: green tests that never covered the case caught nothing.

choices.text: A longer instruction file
choices.why: An instruction file improves the odds; it checks nothing.

choices.text: Running the agent at a lower temperature
choices.why: The current Anthropic API has no temperature, and it would not check anything either.

choices.text: Excluding the tests from the agent's context
choices.why: The tests were not the problem; their coverage was.

hint: Four checks, four findings.

pairs.left: A cart line left with zero mugs
pairs.right: A test written from the docstring

pairs.left: Shipping charged differently after a refactoring
pairs.right: A test pinning the old behaviour
